## Introduction

In recent years, society has stood divided on remote work. Some claim that remote work causes work productivity to slip due to distractions, home activities, etc, while others, have claimed that they feel they are able to work more productively than in the office because they can deal with their home life and work life at the same time. 

Previous studies such as Bloom et al. had found that working from home can improve productivity. Many cited that their gains are believed to have come from  higher job satisfaction and lower quitting rates.

Furthermore, studies like the one Allen et. al @Allenetal performed found that working from home was generally associated with higher job satisfaction, better self-reported productivity, and other mental health benefits.

Finally, meta-analyses such as Gajendran and Harrison @Gajendran found that remote work had beneficial impacts on perceived work life balance. Although, the analysis did find that many remote workers tended to have weaker relationships with their coworkers.

The literature reviewed points to one obvious theme, remote work has its benefits. But the question yet to be answered is: Does remote work's benefits yield the same results for different demographics? 

In this paper, I will attempt to see if remote work's benefits reach across different demographics. I will use an online data set from Kaggle to get my results. I hypothesize that remote work will increase self-perceived productivity across broad demographics.

## Methods

In order to conduct this experiment, I will use results from the Kaggle online data set to create comparisons between remote work respondents and office work respondents. I will specifically focus on the variable: Do you think that working from home increases your work productivity? Additionally, the data set has occupations, years in the workforce, and age group which can also be used to find results. I will use R Studio and AI assistance to do my analyses. 

In my analysis, I intend to compare whether job occupation impacts remote work productivity, whether age impacts remote work productivity, and whether years in the workforce impact work productivity. By comparing these groups, we can find out if perceived productivity productivity increases across demographics. With the results of these analyses, I will be able to answer my hypothesis, and make suggestions for future research.

## Results
```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(123)   # makes simulated p-values reproducible

# NOTE: the CSV must be in the same folder as this .qmd file
df <- read.csv("The Impacts of Working Remotely and in an Office Survey 2.csv") %>%
  rename(productivity = Do.you.think.that.working.from.home.increases.your.work.productivity.,
         arrangement  = Current.Work.Arrangement,
         experience   = Years.of.Experience,
         age          = Age.Group,
         industry     = Industry,
         gender       = Gender)

# Order the age/experience groups correctly (sorted by the first number in each label)
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    prod_bin   = as.integer(productivity == "Yes"),
    age        = factor(age, levels = unique(age)[order(parse_number(unique(age)))]),
    experience = factor(experience, levels = unique(experience)[order(parse_number(unique(experience)))]),
    age_num    = as.numeric(age),
    exp_num    = as.numeric(experience)
  )

# Helper: Cramér's V (effect size) without needing extra packages
cramers_v <- function(tab) {
  chi <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE))$statistic
  unname(sqrt(chi / (sum(tab) * (min(dim(tab)) - 1))))
}

# Helper: format p-values
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# Helper: chi-square test of one predictor vs. productivity
run_chisq <- function(data, var) {
  tab  <- table(data[[var]], data$productivity)
  test <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab))
  simulated <- min(test$expected) < 5          # use simulation if any expected count < 5
  if (simulated) test <- chisq.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)
  tibble(Predictor = var,
         N         = sum(tab),
         ChiSq     = round(unname(test$statistic), 2),
         df        = if (simulated) NA_real_ else unname(test$parameter),
         p         = test$p.value,
         CramersV  = round(cramers_v(tab), 3),
         Simulated = simulated)
}
```



### Work Arrangement


```{r}
#| label: fig-arrangement
#| fig-cap: "Perceived Productivity Benefit by Current Work Arrangement"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(df, aes(x = arrangement, fill = productivity)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Current Work Arrangement",
       y = "Percentage of Respondents",
       fill = "WFH Increases Productivity?") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-arrangement-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Perceived Productivity Benefit by Current Work Arrangement"

df %>%
  group_by(`Work arrangement` = arrangement) %>%
  summarise(N = n(),
            `Said Yes` = sum(prod_bin),
            `% Yes` = round(100 * mean(prod_bin), 1)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pairwise
#| tbl-cap: "Pairwise Comparisons Between Work Arrangements (Holm-Adjusted p-values)"

yes_n <- table(df$arrangement, df$productivity)[, "Yes"]
tot_n <- rowSums(table(df$arrangement, df$productivity))
pw <- pairwise.prop.test(yes_n, tot_n, p.adjust.method = "holm")$p.value

as.data.frame(as.table(pw)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Freq)) %>%
  transmute(`Group 1` = Var1, `Group 2` = Var2, `p (Holm)` = fmt_p(Freq)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llr")
```


The results from the work arrangement section show that those who work remotely and hybrid are 4 to 5 times as likely as in office workers to say working from home boosts productivity. Hybrid and remote workers don't differ from each other. 


### Industry

```{r}
#| label: fig-industry
#| fig-cap: "Perceived Productivity Benefit by Industry"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(df, aes(x = industry, fill = productivity)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Industry",
       y = "Percentage of Respondents",
       fill = "WFH Increases Productivity?") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

In terms of industry, tech is extremely high while retail/hospitality is low. This makes sense given the apparent difficulties with remote work in retail/hospitality.

### Age and Years of Experience

Age and years of experience does not appear to have an effect.

### Summary of Chi-Square Tests

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chisq
#| tbl-cap: "Chi-Square Tests of Perceived Productivity by Predictor"

chisq_results <- map_dfr(c("arrangement", "industry", "experience", "age"),
                         ~ run_chisq(df, .x)) %>%
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))   # correct for running multiple tests

chisq_results %>%
  mutate(Predictor = recode(Predictor,
                            arrangement = "Work arrangement",
                            industry    = "Industry",
                            experience  = "Years of experience",
                            age         = "Age group"),
         p      = fmt_p(p),
         p_holm = fmt_p(p_holm)) %>%
  select(Predictor, N, `χ²` = ChiSq, df, p, `p (Holm)` = p_holm, `Cramér's V` = CramersV) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrr")
```

Work arrangement and industry were significantly associated with perceived productivity, even after Holm correction, whereas age group and years of experience were not (@tbl-chisq)

### Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| label: tbl-logistic
#| tbl-cap: "Logistic Regression Predicting Perceived Productivity Increase (Odds Ratios)"

# Copy of the data with Fully In-Office as the reference group for arrangement
df_model <- df %>%
  mutate(arrangement = relevel(factor(arrangement), ref = "Fully In-Office"))

m <- glm(prod_bin ~ arrangement + experience + industry + age + gender,
         data = df_model, family = binomial)

coefs <- summary(m)$coefficients
ci    <- confint.default(m)   # Wald 95% confidence intervals

tibble(Term = rownames(coefs),
       OR   = exp(coefs[, "Estimate"]),
       `95% CI Lower` = exp(ci[, 1]),
       `95% CI Upper` = exp(ci[, 2]),
       p    = fmt_p(coefs[, "Pr(>|z|)"])) %>%
  filter(Term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(Term = str_replace(Term, "^(arrangement|experience|industry|age|gender)", "\\1: ")) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, align = "lrrrr")
```

In the multivariable logistic regression (@tbl-logistic) work arrangment was the strongest predictor of perceived productivity. Relative to fully in-office workers, fully remote and hybrid workers had substanitally higher odds of reporting productivity increases. Technology workers had higher odds while education workers had one of the lowest odds. Other demographics (age, years of experience, and gender) were not signifcant predictors.
